why: The new checks made the model move many cuts earlier in the sentence (hurt most for mid-length pieces, ≤7–≤10 words) so it began slicing off complements and list items instead of keeping them attached to their heads; this produced the large negative moves in the worst examples while slightly improving very-short bins (≤3). The wording for the single-obligatory-element check was interpreted as encouraging isolation of the completing element on the right, and the noun-head/apposition guidance caused the model to avoid some noun-boundary cuts by shifting cuts into predicates and enumerations.
lesson: When revising, ensure checks discourage cutting between heads and their obligatory complements/appositions (don’t encourage isolating the completer on the right) because otherwise the model will shift cuts earlier and fragment predicates and enumerations, especially harming mid-length pieces.
